strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated task: decoding open-ended, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements, going beyond prior procedural (reading-mode) classification work.

Rigorous experimental design leveraging the OneStop dataset's structure (shared vs. distinct critical spans) to create graded difficulty levels, with a carefully constructed 10-fold cross-validation protocol that separates New Participant, New Text, and New Text&Participant generalization regimes.

Broad and thoughtful model comparison, spanning simple interpretable baselines, adapted SOTA discriminative encoder models (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye), and two newly developed generative multimodal LLM architectures (DalEye-LLaVA, DalEye-Llama), enabling both selection and open-ended reconstruction.

Multiple complementary evaluation metrics for the reconstruction task (question word Kappa, UIUC category Kappa, BLEU, BERTScore, downstream QA accuracy) plus sensible baselines (human alternative questions, arbitrary LLM questions, text-only models) that aid interpretation of an inherently hard-to-evaluate generation task.
Extensive appendix with architecture diagrams, hyperparameter search spaces, prompt variants, and ablations (e.g., fixation- vs word-level input representations) supporting reproducibility.

Appropriate statistical treatment (linear mixed-effects models accounting for non-i.i.d. structure) and honest discussion of limitations and ethical considerations regarding downstream assistive/educational use.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is modest: best 3-way selection accuracy is ~49% (vs 33% chance) and same-critical-span discrimination is barely above chance (57% vs 50%) for the best model, and near chance for most others, tempering the claim of 'considerable success.'

One of the two proposed generative architectures (DalEye-LLaVA) performs essentially at chance across the board, and this negative result is not deeply diagnosed beyond attributing it to prompt/representation choices, weakening confidence in the generative modeling contribution.

In the more practically important New Text regime, DalEye-Llama's reconstructed questions are often no better (and on some metrics worse, e.g. BLEU/BERTScore) than a same-critical-span 'incorrect' human question baseline, suggesting the model may be exploiting span-related lexical cues rather than truly capturing the goal.
No human-performance upper bound is reported for the selection or reconstruction tasks, making it hard to gauge how far current models are from a ceiling achievable from eye movements alone.

Reliance on a single dataset (OneStop, English, Guardian articles, one reading comprehension question format) limits evidence for generalization to other information-seeking scenarios, languages, or reader populations.

The New Text & Participant evaluation regime comprises only ~1% of trials in each split, yielding wide confidence intervals and limiting the reliability of conclusions about the hardest generalization setting.

Limited analysis of which specific eye-movement features (e.g., dwell time on critical span vs. more global/temporal patterns) drive the discriminative models' success, leaving the cognitive interpretability of the results somewhat underexplored despite the paper's stated scientific goals.

The downstream QA-accuracy metric depends on a single fixed QA model (RoBERTa-RACE) whose ceiling (86% correct on ground truth) and idiosyncrasies could bias comparisons across baselines in ways not fully controlled for.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task framing that extends prior 'procedural' goal decoding work (e.g., Hollenstein et al., Shubi et al.) to text-specific, semantically arbitrary information-seeking goals, addressing a previously understudied gap in eye-movement-based cognitive state decoding.
Uses a large, carefully collected eye-tracking dataset (OneStop) with hundreds of text-specific questions and hundreds of participants, giving reasonable scale for this type of study.

Comprehensive experimental design: two heuristic baselines, two adapted SOTA discriminative encoder models, and two newly developed generative multimodal LLMs, evaluated across three generalization regimes (new participant, new text, new participant & text).

Sound statistical methodology: 10-fold cross-validation, linear mixed-effects models accounting for non-i.i.d. structure (repeated participants/paragraphs), and explicit chance-level baselines for each sub-task.

Thoughtful reconstruction evaluation suite (question word match, UIUC category, BLEU, BERTScore, downstream QA accuracy) benchmarked against informative baselines (incorrect human questions, arbitrary LLM questions, text-only model), which helps contextualize otherwise hard-to-interpret generation scores.

Transparent reporting of negative/ablation results (e.g., DalEye-LLaVA at chance, alternative prompts/representations underperforming), and a reasonably thorough ethics and reproducibility discussion.
weaknesses: Effect sizes are modest and the paper's framing ('considerable success', 'progress towards free-form reconstruction') seems to overstate what the numbers show: best 3-way selection accuracy is only 49.3% (chance 33%), and the harder same-critical-span task tops out at 57.3% (chance ~50%), which is a small margin for a task pitched as having strong practical implications.

The free-form reconstruction results reveal that the generative model's apparent competence is almost entirely driven by memorized text-participant associations in the New Participant regime; performance collapses close to chance in the New Text regime (question-word kappa drops from 0.478 to 0.069), undermining the central claim of genuine open-ended goal reconstruction from eye movements rather than memorization of seen texts.

One of the two proposed generative architectures (DalEye-LLaVA) performs at chance across virtually all conditions, which is a significant negative result for half of the paper's 'Models' contribution and raises doubts about the soundness of the eye-movement encoding approach used there.

Despite being billed as 'open-ended' and 'arbitrary', the actual task is still closed-set: each paragraph has exactly 3 pre-authored candidate questions from a fixed pool of 486, and reconstruction is trained/evaluated against a single ground-truth question per trial—this considerably narrows the claimed scope and could mislead readers about the generality of the findings.

No human ceiling/baseline is reported for the selection or reconstruction tasks, making it hard to judge how much headroom remains or how good 49%/57% accuracy actually is relative to an achievable upper bound from eye movements alone.

The core modeling contribution is largely incremental: the discriminative models are adaptations of existing architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye) to a new multiple-choice format, and the generative models are relatively standard integrations of eye-tracking features into existing VLM/LLM backbones (LLaVA-OneVision, Llama 3.1) via LoRA fine-tuning.

The study is confined to a single dataset, single language (English), and a narrow question-generation paradigm (short reading-comprehension-style questions authored by researchers), limiting the generalizability of claims about 'daily life' information-seeking goals invoked in the introduction and discussion.

Some reported comparisons (e.g., generative vs. discriminative models on selection) are somewhat unfair since generative models were not trained explicitly for selection, yet this asymmetry is used to justify model choices without a matched apples-to-apples comparison.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task: decoding arbitrary, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements, going beyond prior work that only classified reading into a small set of pre-defined procedural categories.

Comprehensive experimental design with two task formulations (selection and open-ended reconstruction), multiple model families (heuristic baselines, adapted SOTA discriminative encoders, and two newly developed generative multimodal LLMs), and a principled evaluation protocol with three generalization regimes (new participant, new text, new participant & text) via 10-fold cross-validation.

Careful statistical treatment of the non-i.i.d. nature of the data using linear mixed-effects models, with clearly reported chance baselines for each sub-task (including the subtle Monty-Hall-style chance level for the different-spans task).

Thorough reconstruction evaluation using multiple complementary metrics (question word Kappa, UIUC category Kappa, BLEU, BERTScore, downstream QA accuracy) along with sensible baselines (incorrect human questions, GPT-4o arbitrary questions, text-only model) to contextualize the difficulty of the task and the meaning of the scores.

Strong positioning relative to prior psycholinguistic and NLP work on task-driven reading and cognitive state decoding, with a clear articulation of how this study differs from closely related prior work.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter search spaces, training procedures, model sizes, and appendix architecture diagrams; thoughtful discussion of ethical considerations and application risks.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains, while statistically significant, are still fairly modest in practical terms (e.g., 49.3% vs 33% chance overall, and only 57.3% vs 50% chance in the challenging same-critical-span condition), raising questions about how reliable such decoding would be in real applications at this stage.

One of the two proposed generative models (DalEye-LLaVA) performs essentially at chance across all selection metrics, undermining the claimed contribution of introducing two new generative approaches; only DalEye-Llama shows meaningful signal.

The open-ended reconstruction task shows only modest success and mainly in the easier New-Participant regime; in the more realistic New-Text regime, DalEye-Llama's advantage over simple baselines (e.g., arbitrary GPT-4o/Llama questions) is inconsistent across metrics, tempering the paper's claim of 'meaningful progress' on free-form reconstruction.

Despite the 'open-ended' framing, the underlying task structure is still constrained to exactly three pre-authored candidate questions per paragraph, which may limit how representative the results are of truly unconstrained, naturalistic information-seeking goals.

Reliance on a single dataset (OneStop), single language (English), and a relatively narrow set of paragraph/question materials limits the generality of the conclusions; no cross-dataset or cross-domain validation is provided.

The reproducibility statement leaves the dataset URL blank, and some design choices (e.g., prompt/representation variants for DalEye-Llama) are only explored for one of the two generative models, leaving incomplete ablations for DalEye-LLaVA.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated cognitive/NLP task: decoding open-ended, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements, going beyond prior procedural (small-category) goal decoding work to a semantic, high-cardinality setting.

Comprehensive experimental design with two complementary task formulations (goal selection and goal reconstruction), multiple discriminative and generative model families (including strong adapted SOTA baselines like Haller RNN and RoBERTEye, and novel generative approaches DalEye-Llama/GPT/LLaVA), and a frontier LLM comparison (Gemini zero/few-shot).

Rigorous evaluation protocol: 10-fold cross-validation with three generalization regimes (new participant, new text, new text & participant), appropriate chance-level corrections (Monty Hall-type analysis), and extensive use of mixed-effects models for statistical testing with multiple comparison correction.

Strong grounding in cognitive/psycholinguistic theory, with an interpretability analysis linking model performance to theoretically motivated gaze features (e.g., reading time within/outside critical span), which strengthens scientific credibility and provides converging evidence with prior literature.

Thorough baselining for the generation task (human incorrect questions, arbitrary LLM questions, text-only ablations) that helps isolate the contribution of eye-movement information from textual/lexical shortcuts and pretraining leakage effects.

Extensive supplementary analyses including feature ablations, alternative prompt/representation variants, n-gram overlap analysis to rule out simple lexical matching, and question-category annotation validated against human annotators.
Reasonable ethical discussion regarding potential misuse, bias risks, and consent requirements for future real-world applications.
weaknesses: Performance on goal reconstruction generalizes poorly to new texts (New Text regime), with large drops relative to New Participant, raising questions about the practical utility and true novelty-independence of the eye-movement signal versus memorized associations between paragraphs/questions seen during training.

The task is restricted to single-paragraph, English, silent, screen-based reading in a controlled lab setting with a specific question structure (3 questions per paragraph, 2 sharing a critical span), which may limit generalizability to naturalistic, multi-paragraph or interactive information-seeking scenarios.

DalEye-LLaVA, one of the proposed generative approaches, largely underperforms and is relegated to the appendix, suggesting the embedding-based generative approach is not yet mature, slightly diluting the paper's modeling contribution.

Reliance on commercial/closed models (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-3-Pro-Preview) for both generation and evaluation (e.g., GPT-4o for UIUC categorization) raises reproducibility concerns given potential model updates/deprecation and lack of full transparency into training data overlap.

The improvement of eye-movement-augmented models over text-only baselines, while statistically significant, is sometimes numerically modest (e.g., BLEU differences in the New Text regime), and practical significance for real-world assistive/educational applications remains unproven.

Critical span annotations and question structure are inherited from an existing QA dataset (OneStopQA) rather than newly designed for this study, somewhat limiting the novelty of the underlying data contribution.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated task framing (open-ended, text-specific goal decoding) that goes beyond prior procedural (reading-manner) goal classification work, with a clear formalization into selection and reconstruction sub-tasks.

Uses a large, carefully collected public eye-tracking dataset (OneStop) with a well-designed critical-span annotation scheme that naturally supports two tiers of task difficulty (different vs. same critical span).

Broad and thorough experimental scope: two heuristic baselines, two adapted SOTA discriminative models, three generative approaches (fine-tuned open LLM, fine-tuned commercial LLM, frontier LLM zero/few-shot), plus an additional embedding-based generative model in the appendix.

Rigorous statistical methodology throughout (linear mixed-effects models accounting for non-i.i.d. participant/paragraph structure, multiple comparison corrections, confidence intervals), and systematic evaluation across New Participant/New Text/New Text&Participant generalization regimes.

The cognitive interpretability analysis linking RoBERTEye-Fixations performance to established psycholinguistic constructs (reading time inside vs. outside critical span, comprehension accuracy, paragraph length) is a nice bridge between NLP modeling and cognitive science, and is a distinguishing contribution relative to purely engineering-focused eye-tracking papers.

Extensive, transparent appendix material: feature ablations, alternative prompts/representations, n-gram overlap analysis to rule out simple lexical shortcuts, human-annotator agreement checks for automatic categorization, and detailed reproducibility/hyperparameter documentation.
weaknesses: The headline claim of decoding 'arbitrary' open-ended goals is only convincingly supported in the New Participant regime, where the exact text/question pairs were seen during training; in the New Text regime (the practically relevant, more realistic generalization setting), generative model performance drops sharply and margins over text-only/no-eye-movement baselines shrink substantially, undermining the central motivating claim that eye movements alone reveal specific reading goals for novel content.

Absolute performance on the harder and arguably more scientifically interesting sub-tasks remains modest: same-critical-span selection accuracy is only 57.3% (vs. 50% chance), and reconstruction quality metrics (BLEU, BERTScore) in the New Text regime are low and only marginally better than baselines, raising questions about the practical/scientific significance of the reported 'success.'

The reading-time-informed heuristic baselines perform essentially at chance, suggesting these were weak strawman baselines rather than genuinely competitive alternatives, which somewhat inflates the apparent gap attributable to the more complex neural models.

Reliance on a preview/unreleased frontier model (Gemini-3-Pro-Preview) for a key comparison and for LLM-based question categorization raises reproducibility concerns, since preview models can change or be deprecated, and the GPT-4o-based UIUC category annotation only reaches 86% agreement (κ=0.79) with a single human annotator, a fairly modest validation of an evaluation metric used throughout the paper.

The generative models' gains over text-only counterparts, while statistically significant, are often numerically small in the New Text regime, and it is unclear how much of the 'contribution of eye movements' reflects genuine goal-relevant signal versus incidental correlations (e.g., reading time/length effects) rather than deep decoding of the specific information need.

Novelty relative to the most closely related prior work (Shubi et al., 2025, decoding reading goals) is incremental in some respects — same underlying dataset, similar discriminative architectures adapted rather than newly designed — with the primary innovation being task reframing (semantic vs. procedural) and the addition of generative models, which is a valid but comparatively modest advance for a top-tier venue.

The paper does not include a human baseline/ceiling for the reconstruction task under the same modality-restricted conditions the models face, making it hard to gauge how far models are from an achievable upper bound versus fundamentally limited information content in the gaze signal.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated task: decoding open-ended, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements, clearly distinguished from prior procedural (reading-manner) classification work in the literature review.

Makes clever use of the OneStop dataset's critical-span structure to create a two-tiered difficulty evaluation (different vs. same critical span), providing a Monty-Hall-corrected chance baseline and a genuinely challenging fine-grained discrimination setting.

Comprehensive modeling suite spanning simple interpretable baselines, adapted SOTA discriminative encoders (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye), and multiple generative approaches (fine-tuned Llama/GPT, frontier LLM zero/few-shot, and an LLaVA-based embedding model), giving a thorough picture of the solution space.

Rigorous statistical methodology throughout: mixed-effects models properly accounting for the non-i.i.d. structure of eye-tracking data (repeated participants/paragraphs), with appropriate multiple-comparison corrections.
Systematic evaluation across three generalization regimes (new participant, new text, new participant & text), which is important for assessing real-world applicability rather than memorization.

The cognitive interpretability analysis linking RoBERTEye-Fixations' performance to theoretically motivated gaze features (e.g., reading time within vs. outside critical span) is a nice bridge between NLP modeling and psycholinguistic theory, and produces converging, interpretable findings.

Strong baseline design for goal reconstruction (human-composed incorrect questions, arbitrary LLM questions, text-only fine-tuned variants) that helps isolate the specific contribution of eye-movement information from textual/pretraining priors.

Extensive appendix with ablations (feature ablation for RoBERTEye, prompt/representation variants for DalEye-Llama), reasonable reproducibility documentation, and an n-gram overlap analysis validating the inferential (non-extractive) nature of the QA task.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains modest in practical terms: 49.3% vs. 33% chance for 3-way selection, and only 57.3% vs. 50% chance for the same-critical-span condition, which somewhat tempers claims of 'considerable success,' especially for real-world assistive/educational applications discussed in the introduction and discussion.

Goal reconstruction performance degrades substantially in the New Text regime relative to New Participant, and the New Participant regime's strong results could partly reflect memorization of text-question pairings from LLM pretraining/fine-tuning on OneStopQA materials rather than genuine goal decoding from eye movements, despite the text-only control conditions.

DalEye-LLaVA underperforms notably relative to DalEye-Llama and is not thoroughly diagnosed; its inclusion mainly as a 'reference point for future work' weakens the paper's generative modeling narrative.

The UIUC question-category annotation quality check relies on agreement with a single human annotator (one of the paper's authors) on only 100 samples, which is a fairly weak validation of this evaluation metric.

The feature ablation study for RoBERTEye-Fixations shows generally small and often non-significant effect sizes, suggesting substantial redundancy across feature groups, which weakens the strength of conclusions that can be drawn about which specific eye-movement signals drive decoding.

The cognitive-interpretability analysis is performed only for the single best-performing discriminative model, not extended to the generative models or compared across model types, limiting the generality of the cognitive insights.
Single dataset, single language (English), and a narrow genre (Guardian news articles) constrain claims about generalizability of the approach to other domains or reading contexts.
Reproducibility statement contains unfilled placeholders for dataset/code URLs in the submitted version, which is a minor but notable oversight for a paper emphasizing reproducibility.
